title: That you may believe (John 20:24–31)
hookLine: Thomas says my Lord and my God, and John tells us why he wrote
last: GLAD, WHEN THEY SAW THE LORD.

lines: UNLESS I SEE, I WILL NOT BELIEVE.
cards: One of the twelve wasn't in the room that Sunday. Thomas, called the twin. When the others tell him, we have seen the Lord, he gives a no that people still quote.
Unless I see the nail prints, and put my finger in them, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe. Later readers nicknamed him Doubting Thomas. The Gospel never calls him that.
And a week later, he's the one who says the words this Gospel opened with, to Jesus's face.

teach.h: EIGHT DAYS LATER, THOMAS IS THERE.
teach.b: Eight days later they're in the room again, doors shut, and this time Thomas is there. Jesus stands among them, says peace be with you, and turns straight to Thomas.
He offers exactly what Thomas asked for: reach here your finger, behold my hands, reach your hand into my side. Be not faithless, but believing.

teach.h: THE TEXT NEVER SAYS HE TOUCHED.
teach.b: Here's what's striking: the text never says Thomas touched him. Painters, like Caravaggio, show his finger in the wound. John doesn't.
What John records is the answer. In the King James Bible: "And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God." This Gospel began: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God.
Now, near the end, the disciple who asked for proof says it to his face.

teach.h: MY LORD AND MY GOD: FULL CIRCLE.
teach.b: Full circle. Then Jesus: "blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed." That line is about everyone after Thomas, everyone reading.

teach.h: WHY JOHN WROTE: THAT YOU MIGHT HAVE LIFE.
teach.b: Then John tells you why he wrote: "many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book: But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name."

teach.h: BLESSED ARE THEY THAT HAVE NOT SEEN.
teach.b: That you might have life. It reads like an ending, and some readers think it once was one, with chapter twenty-one added after.
Tradition says Thomas later carried the news east, as far as India, where the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala trace their church to him.

how: Many churches read the story of Thomas on the Sunday after Easter, and Christians in India's Saint Thomas tradition honor him as the apostle who brought them the faith.

games.q: what's inside John 20:24–31 — tap the pairs.

s: John's Gospel calls him Doubting Thomas
the nickname came later. the text calls him Thomas, called Didymus.
the text says Thomas put his finger in the wounds
Jesus invites him to, but John records only his answer: my Lord and my God.
John says he left many other signs out of his book
"many other signs truly did Jesus... which are not written in this book."

games.q: you're Thomas. the risen Jesus stands in front of you and offers his wounds. what do you do?
o: reach out and touch the wounds first.
say: my Lord and my God.
games.why: John records only his answer: "My Lord and my God." whether he touched, the text doesn't say.

practice: Let verse thirty-one come slowly, these are written, that ye might believe, and that believing ye might have life through his name, then say the last part again: that ye might have life.
Let it sit beside whatever you're hungry for right now, more energy, more meaning, more joy. If you pray, ask for that life; if you have doubts, Thomas's honesty is welcome here too.

wordCard.voice: Thomas. The disciple who doubted until he saw, and then said, my Lord and my God, to Jesus's face.
